newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FORECAST-Rand, low base to push January PPI higher.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Rand, low base to push January PPI higher.

text.p: The lagged effects of the rand's weakness last year coupled with technical factors should push producer inflation almost a percent higher in January from December, economists said on Friday.
A Reuters consensus forecast of 10 economists forecast the Producer Price Index (PPI), due for release at 0900 GMT next Thursday, would rise 1.0 percent month-on-month or 9.4 percent year-on-year.
The average was drawn from a range of 0.7 to 1.1 percent.
"It should be higher because of the effects of imported prices and a low base a year ago," Nedcor economist Magan Mistry said.
The rand lost more than a fifth of its value on a trade-weighted basis last year, while PPI in January 1996 rose just 0.4 percent month-on-month.
The effect's of the rand's pummeling last year brought pressure to bear on the imported component of the index last month, forcing it 1.8 percent higher from November and up 9.3 percent year-on-year.
"In December the year-on-year imported component shot up," Econometrix economist Tony Twine said. "If that holds into January, it increases the pain of the year-on-year for January."
He added that normal beginning-of-the-year price increases, such as electricity, would also exert upward pressure on the index.
Economists also pointed to the fact that the consumer price index, which had become a leading indicator for PPI, had also signalled a healthy month-on-month increase could be in store.
CPI rose 1.3 percent month-on-month in January.
Standard Bank economics division noted that January was a high survey month, and that some pressure was likely to be brought to bear from a number of categories surveyed quarterly in January.
"The most important of these (in terms of their weights within the PPI) are paper and pulp, chemicals and rubber and plastics," the bank said.
Paper and pulp make up 2.3 percent of the overall index, chemical and chemical products 9.54 percent and rubber and plastics 1.36 percent.
EW Balderson economist Mike Schussler said the current upward trend in producer inflation was expected to peak in March this year, when he expected the annual rate to come in at around 10.5 percent.
"After that it should drop quite substantially giving an average of around 9.4 percent for the year," Schussler said.
